text: Here is a sentence that sounds like jargon: a matrix is a linear transformation. Most people learn matrices as grids of numbers with a fiddly multiplication rule, and the rule never seems to mean anything. In this lesson we will watch what a matrix does instead, by letting it move every point of the plane at once, and the rule will fall out of the picture almost by itself.

A transformation is just a function that takes in a vector and hands back another vector. The word transformation is chosen on purpose, because it invites you to picture motion, with every arrow swinging from its starting position to its new one. Watching every arrow at once would be a mess, so picture only their tips, as if each point of the grid were a dot of paint that slides to wherever the function sends it.

Most functions would crumple the grid like a sheet of wet paper, bending its lines into curves. A linear transformation is far better behaved. Its grid lines stay straight, they stay parallel, and they stay evenly spaced, while the origin stays exactly where it was. You can think of it as a sheet of graph paper that may be stretched or slanted, but is never bent or torn.

That rigid behaviour has a remarkable consequence. Take the vector two, one, which means two copies of i hat plus one copy of j hat. After the transformation the grid lines are still evenly spaced, so the vector lands at two copies of wherever i hat landed, plus one copy of wherever j hat landed. The recipe survives the move. So to know where every vector goes, you only need to follow two arrows, i hat and j hat.

Let us watch a particular example. Suppose i hat lands on the point two, one, and j hat lands on the point minus one, one. Watch the whole grid carry those two arrows with it. The yellow vector rides along, and it ends up at two times the new i hat, plus one times the new j hat, which is the point three, three.

Those four numbers describe the transformation completely, so we write them in a little box. The first column is where i hat lands, and the second column is where j hat lands. That box is the matrix. It is not a mysterious table; it is a record of where the two basis arrows went, written down column by column.

Now the multiplication rule is easy to read. To multiply the matrix by a vector x, y, take x copies of the first column and y copies of the second column, and add them. That is exactly the recipe we just watched on the grid. The row by row rule you may have memorised gives the same numbers, but the column picture tells you why it works.

With that reading, any matrix can be turned back into a motion. If the first column is zero, one, and the second is minus one, zero, then i hat swings up and j hat swings left, and the whole plane turns a quarter of a circle. If i hat stays put and j hat leans over to one, one, the plane is sheared, like a deck of cards pushed sideways. And if both columns lie on the same line, the entire plane is flattened onto that line, which is the span of the columns from the last lesson.

This is what happens inside a language model, only in many more dimensions. A layer holds a weight matrix, and multiplying an embedding vector by it moves that vector to a new place in a new space, where each column says where one input direction is sent. Training, in the end, is a search for matrices that move words to useful places.

So a matrix is a record of where i hat and j hat land, and multiplying by it means rebuilding a vector from those landing spots. The next question is what happens when you apply one transformation and then another, and that, in the next lesson, is what matrix multiplication really means.
